name: Neural therapy

lead: Neural therapy is a practice in which local anaesthetic is injected into particular body sites, including scars, nerves and trigger points, to treat chronic pain and illness. Practitioners say it normalises a dysfunctional autonomic nervous system.

Its link to appearance is indirect: some skin conditions such as notalgia paresthetica have been treated with it, and scars are among the sites injected. It is practised mainly in Europe and South America.

paras: A trained clinician injects a small amount of local anaesthetic, often procaine or lidocaine, at chosen sites in the skin, scars or around nerves, across a series of sessions. Not a self-treatment.
Needle damage to organs is a described risk, and a case report describes brainstem hemorrhage after treatment. The American Cancer Society states evidence does not support use for cancer.

angle.text: Practitioners inject scars and skin areas, and published work covers an itchy skin condition. It is not an established cosmetic treatment.

lead: Neural therapy is a form of alternative medicine in which local anaesthetic is injected at specific body sites to treat chronic pain and illness.[1] A review in a rehabilitation journal describes injection of local anaesthetics into scars, peripheral nerves, autonomic ganglia, trigger points and glands, aiming to normalise a dysfunctional autonomic nervous system.[2]

Practitioners treat scars and skin sites, so people interested in skin or scar appearance meet it in that context, and a 2024 study examined neural therapy in notalgia paresthetica, an itchy skin condition.[3] The International Medical Association of Neural Therapy has about 400 members, and a 2007 survey found it among the most used alternative techniques by German family physicians.[1]
Trials have tested it mainly for pain, with mixed findings, while Wikipedia characterises it as pseudoscience and cites studies finding no benefit.[1]

paras: In 1925 German surgeon Ferdinand Huneke gave his sister a procaine-containing drug for severe migraines, injected it intravenously rather than as recommended, and the attack stopped.[1] He and his brother Walter then used Novocaine for various ailments.[1] In 1940 an injection into a leg scar relieved a painful shoulder, which Huneke called the secondary phenomenon.[1] Later segment therapy injected skin areas linked to internal organs.[1]
Procaine was first synthesised in 1905 by Alfred Einhorn and sold as Novocain.[4]

Proponents believe interference fields at certain body sites produce an energy causing illness, and that injection can disrupt them.[1] Authors in the field describe autonomic dysfunction as the underlying driver.[2]

A 2023 scoping review of low-dose local anaesthetics identified 129 studies, mostly on chronic pain.[5] A randomized trial of 104 patients with cervical myofascial pain compared kinesio taping, trigger-point injection and neural therapy.[6] A 2024 randomized observer-blind trial found low inter-rater reliability for neck reflex points used to find interference fields, but increased pressure pain thresholds after therapy.[7] A 2024 article reported neural therapy in notalgia paresthetica.[3] A case series followed 280 refractory chronic pain patients after therapeutic local anaesthesia.[8]

The American Cancer Society states the evidence does not support use for cancer or other diseases, and Edzard Ernst argued in 2007 that risks such as needle damage to organs outweigh possible benefit.[1] A reported case describes brainstem hemorrhage after neural therapy for decreased libido.[1]
